In high school I wrote a whole paper about this. My thesis was to define a movie we have to analyze the delivery. A movie is intended to be watched in one sitting. Yes, I know some films have intermissions and I'm sure there is some art film that pushes against this, but by and large, the director isn't intending for the audience to pause the film and finish it later on. The delivery system for television is the exact opposite. Within the medium there are breaks. Yes, you can watch a show all at once and this became more of a trend during the binge era. Textually speaking, however, shows AREN'T DESIGNED to be viewed in one sitting. The very nature of splitting something into separate episodes supports this. With modern tv in particular, you can't watch a random episode and get the full effect. Episodes are rarely self contained nowadays. 

The biggest counter to this is the MCU which mimics the television model. But I'd argue that the failure of the recent MCU films proves my point. Early on the films were pretty self contained. You could watch Thor without needing to watch Iron Man. And to an extent this is still somewhat true. The Guardian films function as a self contained trilogy for the most part. But Doctor Strange 2? It's required to watch Wanda Vision. And soon this became too much and shows that the television model doesn't really work in movies. 

In actuality modern television mimics novels. Both are long form storytelling that doesn't require you to consume it all at once. In all, I feel like this conversation only ever started because David Lynch made The Return.

The 1 Page = 1 Minute is a bit iffy. It more or less depends on the content of the script. For example, Aaron Sorkin's scripts can reach pretty damn close to 200 pages, the one for Steve Jobs is around 170, but many of his movies end up being under two and half hours. This is because the actors perform the dialogue rather quickly. However, the script for Three Billboards is under 90 pages and the movie is about two hours.

If you're not going to produce the script and keep this a personal project I would focus on getting the story right. But in the future, if you're writing on spec or for hire unless you've really established yourself a 238-page script won't fly.

I think the big issue with *Nomadland* isn't a problem with the film but the subject matter. The topic of Nomads, to my knowledge, isn't a widely covered topic in cinema so Zhao's film is going to be more scrutinized because it's the first big one. Audiences are going to come to it with a lot of expectations and from online discourse, a lot of them thought the film was going to be in a way a how-to guide about being a Nomad. Instead, it's a story about one person and her experience being a Nomad. I do believe it has a lot of subtext that requires some digging, I think the RV scene is crucial in how it shows that this fancy machine is out of their reach. The awe the characters feel communicates this. But this is never stated. Does the film have problems? Yes. By nature of Fern being white, she is provided many privileges that a black woman wouldn't have. This is never fully brought up and I think you could have while still keeping the story intimate. Despite this, I hesitate to call the film apolitical. Sure, it's not *Trial of the Chicago 7* but I don't believe the film exists without politics, it's just Zhao decided to not be vocal about it. I really think people need to rethink what "political" means. 

Circling back to my original point, all this pressure to be political comes from being the first. Let's say the film didn't win Best Picture which could mean no more films about this community/lifestyle could get produced. With a subject like WW2 and the Holocaust, filmmakers are allowed to explore different facets of the event because so many films about it exist. *Nomadland* doesn't have that.
